utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were yesterday in volume 1 at tab 9. I wonder if the witness could take up volume 1 and turn to tab 10. This is a report or -- yes, it's a report of yours of the 16th of March. The second page in the English, and second page in the -- no, first page in the Bosnian. Right at the foot of the page. We see that you deal with the protests of the Siptars, as you describe them, 3.000 people carrying pictures of Mother Teresa, and with slogans roughly equal to "Stop the Serbian terror." I think you will recognise, Mr. Delic, that there are different views about the history of what happened in Kosovo. Where the Kosovo Albanians carried placards saying something like "Stop the Serbian terror," was it entirely fictional or was there something that they were able to refer to by that term?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was born in Kosovo and Metohija and I lived there at the time, one cannot say that there were any indications of what you would call Serbian terror. On a day-to-day basis, there were all kinds of demonstrations. If you just look one passage below what you've just read. I signed this paper, I think. Yes, I did. Nobody addressed the demonstrators. There was just one person filming them on camera. The person with the camera also had a goal of their own. The picture of the demonstrations was supposed to tour the world for propaganda purposes. And as you can see from here, nobody tried to prevent this rally. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on the next page, if you are still following me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because I've let you answer at length and we must be somewhat focused. I just want to know, and I'm not concerned about the answer, I just want to know what your position is. Was there anything at all that Serbs had done to Kosovo Albanians that could explain why they carried placards saying "Stop the Serbian terror," or was it entirely fictional? I hope the question's easy for you to understand.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was something that was orchestrated and imposed from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Completely fictional.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pure fiction. People were living freely whichever way they liked. Can I just say one more thing? While we are on this page 10, look at paragraph 2, the second line, 12th and 13th of March. On several occasions fire was opened at Serbian and Montenegrin houses. Among other things, fire was opened on this occasion on my house, and that is written here. It was the house of my father. My neighbour's house was targeted too. It was certainly not a rally. The houses of my brothers were also targeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to tab 14, please. This is where it can be dealt with very briefly with reference to expression of fear by the -- it's on page 1, towards the foot of the page in English, just before paragraph 2. And you can find that on page 1, and it says: "It's very likely that these actions are being carried out by KLA members. There are those who plant rumours among the local Albanians that their hay barns are being burned by Chetniks and Arkan's Army." And you made an observation in your evidence about that and about the impossibility of that. You say it's impossible that their hay barns were being burnt by anyone. Whether Chetniks or Arkan's army not being the point, but do you say it's impossible that their hay barns were being burned, hay and barns?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, just one correction, if I may. You've just read that somebody was burning their villages and hay barns. It's not a village. It's hay. That should be corrected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, is this just made up altogether?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That somebody was burning their hay and their barns is not true, because this was going on on the ground. But if there had been Arkan's troops or some sort of Chetniks, that was absolutely impossible. This was designed to create fear among Albanians who did not join the KLA and to force them in this way to join the KLA, because a considerable number of Albanians at the time was against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just move on to tab 16, and we'll look at that briefly. It's an order of yours, I think, or a report of yours. A report of yours. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the previous answer, the beginning of the answer, somebody was burning their hay and barns, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it was in respect of tab 16, it may not be in the document itself, but it was when you were telling us about tab 16 that you told us this in answer to the accused: "Any contact with civilians --" this is speaking of yourself, or the army. "Any contact with civilians is outside the competencies of the army. That's something that the police is authorised to do. They can check identities, and they can issue warnings, but the army doesn't do that." You said that in the context of a question about journalists, but does this answer of yours, given in relation to a document that was March 1998, reflect again the recognition that in the absence of a state of emergency, the army and the civilians have nothing to do with one another?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what you just quoted on another occasion, but I can answer this question as well. It's all the same. First of all, you see that there is no army involved in this operation. Tab 16 refers to a purely MUP activity. In the army, there is a part of the troops called the unit of the military police, and they have the same powers as MUP. They, therefore, are authorised to contact with citizens in relation to certain acts. But as for contact between the army and civilians, that applies to operations involving combat. If the army were acting in support of the MUP, then it was the MUP who had direct contact with civilians. But I'm not saying we never had any contact. I personally contacted civilians. Why wouldn't I if I know their language and they understand me and if we need to communicate about a particular thing? But due to the nature of the MUP's job, it was always they who contacted with the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just looking at tab 16 itself, by the way, before I move to my next point, and the Court can see it at the first page, as can you, Mr. Delic, it says this: "It was characteristic that there were foreign journalists in the sector where the operation was carried out, probably inside the houses of terrorists, filming only when MUP members opened fire and took action and the population fleeing from the surrounding villages to the woods. They did not film the actions of the terrorists," in relation to a particular incident. Is it your belief and position that foreign journalists were always capable of being deceived, or is it your position that they were engaged in some kind of conspiracy to advance false accounts? What is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that there are all sorts of journalists. I believe I mentioned a journalist here, Sali Beqe [phoen], who took the liberty of actually crossing the state border together with the terrorists in a group that was combatting our border units. So there were all sorts of journalists, including freelancers who write independently to reporters of particular televisions and newspapers. On the 17th of July, 1998, as terrorists were attacking Orahovac, one foreign television filmed this, and I have some of their recordings. So there were journalists who would come to the country in all sorts of ways, legally or illegally, and then followed the terrorists in their activities. This applies especially to journalists and televisions from Albania, because they, in their news bulletins, regularly reported on events from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to so-called Western, which I suppose means American and Western European journalists, do you say that they were all misled by the KLA or that they were all involved in a conspiracy?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can never lump everyone together and say that they were all part of a conspiracy. There were television companies and newspapers who objectively tried to monitor events in our country, but there were also journalists, especially from Albania, who write -- who wrote in a biased way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... journalism, there was a television programme produced in Serbia called The Serb Version of the Split, I think, in 2000. Did you see that programme? I think it was in probably more than one part. Did you see that programme?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which television showed that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time also?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't recall the date and time at the moment, but is it critical? Can you remember a programme that was The Serb Version of the Split?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if this programme was in 2000, I did watch certain programmes but not in 2000. I watched them in 2004.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1998, what position was General Pavkovic in relation to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, General Pavkovic was the commander of the Pristina Corps, and I was commander of the 549th Brigade. He was my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course General Perisic was the Chief of the General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Perisic was at the time Chief of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just look at a couple of very short clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the transcripts are available. Your Honour, these are clips 8 and 9 we're going to be looking at at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that was, we saw, General Pavkovic, and what he said was that the attitude of the General Staff was that the army shouldn't interfere in those matters. Terrorism is to be dealt with by MUP. Can we look at the next one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we there saw the Chief of the General Staff explaining that the army was waiting for a decision from the Assembly and from the Supreme Defence Council before the army could get involved. Was that your understanding on the ground of what was happening? He [Realtime transcript read in error "you"] said that the decisions were blocked by Milosevic. Was that your understanding of the position on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, the situation on the ground was so hard, and of course I lived it every day, unlike Perisic who visited the territory of Kosovo and Metohija maybe once a month. May I describe to you my meeting with Perisic in this context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just to correct the transcript which has you said that the decisions were blocked by Milosevic which should be he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, he said the decision, yes -- Your Honour is quite right, the decisions were blocked by Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to your suggestion of mentioning your encounter with Perisic, what date?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in end May 1998 when he came to visit my unit together with the commander of the 3rd Army, General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll take that when we reach -- if it's material, we'll at least take it when we reach May of 1998, but at the moment -- well, just two things. You explained that you looked at television programmes in 2004, presumably when you were preparing evidence. Did you see this programme containing these and other interviews with Pavkovic and Perisic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The programme that I saw in 2004 was called The War That Could Have Been Avoided, and you can see a lot of foreign protagonists in that programme, people who had a considerable and negative impact on the aggression on Yugoslavia. But those short excerpts that you just showed, I had occasion to see them already, but probably not in 2000; a bit later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just simply want to know, do they depict maybe the frustration of the army on the ground, that everyone was waiting for action to be taken to allow the army to intervene?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the army was not frustrated. The army, just as the population in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, was seriously endangered by terrorism. Incidents were happening on the road. A large chunk of territory was controlled by terrorists. Murders happened on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your account the army didn't and indeed couldn't intervene, could it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, and this talks also about the beginning of 1998, we reported to our superiors. You can see these reports under tabs 10 to 16. All of these are my reports to the corps commander, and it always says "Attention: Corps commander or Chief of Staff," so they should know how hard the situation is in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's see how things developed. If we can look now, please, at clip 11. This is going to be Pavkovic, again, following a passage by a narrator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, same television programme, something that you've seen before. Something that you've seen before, Mr. Delic, this passage?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've seen this before, the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what General Pavkovic made clear is that during 1998 the circle of hatred was spreading, executions and mass graves were increasing, and the VJ was getting involved in various ways. One is logistic, but it was also getting involved, in 1998, by support with arms fire in specific regions. Well, now, first of all, is General Pavkovic right that in 1998 the army was giving fire support to the police?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let me just correct what you've said at the very outset. Now you're saying what the commentator said here. You're saying that General Pavkovic said it. It was the broadcaster who said hatred was spreading, that there were a lot of killings. General Pavkovic was only saying -- that has to be distinguished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What General Pavkovic said is quite correct. It pertains to the second half of 1998, when practically half of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija was under the control of the terrorists and when the terrorists held practically all the roads in Kosovo and Metohija and hindered not only military transportation but also civilians could not freely travel in their own country. They would be kidnapped, especially Serbs and Albanians who were loyal citizens of Serbia and who worked in state institutions. In a country that was free, no one could travel from Prizren to Pristina or from Pec to Pristina and be sure that they would not be killed or kidnapped along the way. I fully agree with everything that General Pavkovic said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move chronologically so far as I'm able to arrange that. Would you be good enough to go to tab 17. We still don't have a translation of this. Oh, yes, we do. This is just a question about a document, because I think this may have been the first document where we explored the certification by Colonel Markovic, which we see at the end of the document, and in respect of which you explained that Markovic was one of those who produced these excerpts, this and the subsequent one. I'm not really interested in the document itself particularly, save for this: If we look at the original of the document, as you'll be looking at it, and if the learned Judges observe what can be seen in the various markings on the English, we'll see that the material has simply been redacted, blanked out, so that we only see part of the document. Now, what's all that about, or are you quite unable to tell us?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you because I was interested in the same thing. This is a document from the security administration. This document was submitted to the Prosecutor's office over two years ago. I submitted it to the investigator who was investigating Siptar crimes. As for this that is blanked out, Mr. Markovic made an excerpt from this document, from those parts of security reports that pertain to my zone only. As for what is blanked out, it was said that all portions where names are mentioned of Siptars who cooperated with the service, in order to protect them, and also -- their names would be blanked out, and also their places of residence so they could not be identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if it ever occurred to the commission or the committee group of officers sitting around the table or anybody else doing this exercise in document production that the question of whether names of informers should be available to the Prosecution would -- should ultimately, in courts like this, be a matter for the court itself? Did that ever occur to anybody preparing this material?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the security service is concerned, they have their own methods, and I'm not aware of them. They have their own connections. They have their own informers, and they're duty-bound to protect them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It didn't occur to them or to you or to anybody else that the question of redacting documents, and although this relates to a KLA issue in 1998 and may not be material, there's redactions right through these documents, never occurred to anyone that this was a matter that ought first to be raised with the court to see if these documents could be presented in redacted form?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was written or, rather, prepared for the Prosecutor's office, and the investigator who talked to me about this absolutely did not insist on knowing who these informers were. Discovering the names of the informers would quite simply mean their death. Anyway, many persons who cooperated with Serbs or the state organs of Serbia in 1998 and 1999 were killed, all the way up to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the point I'm trying to make through the witness and he hasn't answered it, I'm not going to ask it again, may be a point that relates to range of documents where you'll find editing marks of the same kind. I'll draw your attention to them from time to time. You've probably already seen them in the papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move on now, please, to tab 20. Now, again, I'm not particularly interested in tab 20 itself. We can scan it indeed. It's an interim report on a border incident, and we can see its format which has participants in the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the Court goes over to the second page, it sees a narrative of events set out with names and places and activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, is this form of report by the military - it's a report of your brigade - is this report a standard form of report for a serious incident?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the documents you could see the different types of reports that existed, but it's important that participants in the event concerned are referred to, the description of the event concerned, and the measures taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course in the event of casualties, fatalities or injuries, they are identified. In the event of --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is any such thing, then an investigating judge is called in. The investigating judge comes to the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the army, if it's involved as it was at this border incident, will have provided a full and detailed report, built on all its records, setting out its version of what happened.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the incident was on the border, then the local mixed commission was also informed. These commissions had their own sectors. Here it is commission number 4 that calls from the other side the Albanian local commission number 4 to attend the on-site investigation with regard to that particular incident. That was the type of practice that existed in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the reason I ask you this question is as follows: Racak was outside your area, wasn't it? Not very far outside, but it was outside.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've seen the senior policeman, now General, Radosavljevic, making it clear that the VJ were involved at Racak. That's not for you to decide. It's for the Judges, of course. But if the VJ were involved in a proper operation at Racak, would it be reasonable to assume that a report of at least this detail should exist somewhere in the army files?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different reports in relation to Racak. I believe that the commander of the army unit, whose individual members were not in Racak but in the immediate vicinity of Racak but on the other side of the road in cooperation with the OSCE agreement, will come to this courtroom and testify. But I talked to the OSCE people, Krsman Jelic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Commander of the 243rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And his report, have you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just add what's missing from the transcript? The witness said General Krsman Jelic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is impossible to record everything that's said if there is more than one speaker at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am commander of one brigade, he is the commander of another brigade. I simply see no reason for me to read his reports. As for Mr. Guri, he was commander, or perhaps not even a full-fledged commander but the leader of a unit that was of a lower rank. He could not even have communication with the army. At that time he held the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as for the MUP is concerned, it is the head of the Secretariat of the Ministry of the Interior from Urosevac that can speak about this particular action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for the answers you've given. All I wanted from you. When you were dealing with tab 21, we needn't revisit it, it's a video, but you did make the point that the 53rd Border Battalion based in Djakovica and directly attached to the Pristina Corps was responsible to you in the disciplinary sense because it was based in the same barracks. Now, you didn't go on to amplify that, but perhaps you just could explain that. What were your range of responsibilities for the 53rd Border Battalion based in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 53rd Border Battalion based in Djakovica was in my barracks. He -- it received orders from the Pristina Corps and sent reports to the Pristina Corps. However, since it is in my barracks, as for the discipline of its soldiers in the barracks and in town, it was responsible to my battalion commander who was in the Djakovica garrison. Further on, I was responsible for their logistics, for their supplies, because they had very small logistics units of their own, and it is from my warehouses that they got food, weapons, clothing, and whatever else they needed. Another responsibility I had in respect of that battalion was that if that unit is attacked on the border with strong forces, that I give them assistance. As for discipline and as for logistics, they were responsible towards me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So if they did something wrong, you'd be the person who would have to discipline them.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only my unit had the military police. So all events, border incidents and others, were dealt with by my military police unit. They documented it and they reported it to the Pristina Corps regardless of whether it had to do with my unit or the 53rd Border Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was -- were they co-extensive with what -- was their area co-extensive with yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were responsible for the border only. In my barracks in Djakovica, they had only a small part of their personnel. I think they had about 12 border posts. We could count them here. They had border posts that were taken up all the time, and they had the type of border posts that we called summer border posts in the mountains. Most of the personnel of that battalion was on the border posts all the time providing security for the border, and only a small part, the intervention company and the training company for training young border soldiers who came to do their military service at the border, only they were in my barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just this: All their border posts were within your general area of responsibility, or did they extend beyond it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the border posts were in my zone, or to be more precise, from Mitar Vojinovic, which is a border post on the north, all the way down to the border post of Likane, which is near Mount Pastrik. Those border posts of theirs were in my zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ones that were outside of your responsibility, were they further to the north? On which side?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were to the north, further to the north, from Mitar Vojinovic, the next one is Morina, then Kosare, Koznjar, and so on and so forth. Then further up north and towards Mount Prokuplje, its highest peak Djerevica, that was in the area of responsibility of the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tab 22, please. Now, this document, which we looked at briefly, is an order for the deployment of stand-by forces. And if we go to 3.2, it says on English page 2, set up in-depth state border security, and in a joint action with the MUP and the 549, block routes and then smash and destroy the DTG and other forces. Did this order at this date represent a change of gear for the involvement of the army in any way?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no change. This is an order which meant that the army left the barracks for the first time to three different localities. As far as my brigade is concerned, they went to three different localities outside the barracks. If necessary, we can find the right map and show this on the map, because we've already had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're now engaged in smashing, as we can see, and destroying the DTG and other forces. How were you doing that, by the ambush points on the borders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't read this right. This is the first time that the troops went out into the area, and it says that the troops should be on the ready, standing by for in-depth security of the state border and for dealing with possible attacks on military facilities and smashing forces in Koritnik, Suva Reka, Pastrik and so on, in concert with the MUP of Serbia. That is the only thing that is referred to here, that the army should be on the ready, but they do not have to engage in such activity. Everything that is mentioned here has to do with the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was reading, I thought -- maybe the translation is a problem, but I was reading from 3.2 and I thought it said -- or it says in English "smash and destroy the DTG and other groups," and that was the order, I think. Does this not amount to an order to relate to whoever you could find in the form of that group?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said you were reading 3.2, paragraph 3.2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3.2 does not pertain to my unit. It pertains to the 55th Border Battalion, and 55th Border Battalion is on the state border itself, since weapons were being carried over very intensively and all their activities are geared towards preventing this bringing in of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, as to your group, what was your group's functions? Shall we go over to 4.2.1?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my decision, from point 4.1 until 4.2.3. My units are given an assignment here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see the same language there, don't we, in 4.2.1. Your units were to smash the forces of armed rebellion and infiltrated DTG on the following axis: Pastrik-Prizren-Suva Reka. Had the intention already become clear to eliminate people when you found them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're even misreading this text. What is a key point here is to be on stand-by, on the ready. And then it says here for what; for in-depth security of the state border. That is the first task. The second one is intervene in the direction of threatened military features. And then it's the depot of Ljubizda, the depot of Djinovci, and the barracks, and smash the forces of armed rebellion and infiltrated groups on the following axes, those that lead from the border to the territory in-depth. So until the 17th of July the army was not engaged at all and this is dated the 22nd of April, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, 4.5.5, or the second to last point on this document. 4.5.5, please. The preparation with anti-nuclear, chemical and biological measures. Were there biological measures within your brigade's capacity and capability?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course such things do not exist in my country at all let alone in my brigade. How could I have them in my brigade? These are general measures in terms of anti-nuclear, chemical and biological defence, self-reliance, relying on one's own resources that every stand-by soldier has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just go to the last part of the document, very last sentence. "File reports every day at 0600 hours --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nice is putting questions improperly, and the witness did not notice that. Mr. Nice is talking about some kind of weapons, but this does not have to do with weapons at all. These are protective measures from chemical weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood what Mr. Nice was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness answered. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last part of the document is: "File reports every day at 0600 hours on the situation at 0530, and to the duty operations officer at 2200 hours on the situation at 2100 hours, and interim ones as necessary." Was that the sort of standard of daily reporting that you expected from your subordinate groups throughout the various incidents that you've been telling us, telling us of?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that at this time incidents occurred only at the border. This is customary form. The time of reporting is given, and then this reporting that is referred to here is oral, by telephone, and there have to be these deadlines so that written reports could be sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We would then have passed over or reached Ashdown. Unfortunately, I find that I've not mislaid but I must have left in my room some of the papers I need for that so I'll come back to it after the break. But we can move on to tab 45, which is potentially related and we'll come back to Ashdown after the break. Would you go to tab 45, please. Now, here is a very urgent document, and it comes from Major General Negosav Nikolic, and it goes to the -- from the command at the Pristina Corps. He says this: "Considering that it is expected that numerous delegations of diplomatic representatives, observer missions, representatives of humanitarian organisations -" and so on - "will visit the territory of Kosovo, and as they tour certain areas according to their own plans and without announcement, in order to prevent opening fire on the sectors in which the said persons might happen to be..." You then go on to say the following or, rather, the order goes on to say the following: "... prohibit opening fire from artillery weapons... without the approval of the Corps Command. "Fire may be opened from other types of weapons only if the brigade commander deems this appropriate in order to neutralise targets that are a threat to human lives, such as: bunkers, buildings in which there are no civilians and other facilities from which fire is opened from mortars and other weapons ..." And then in 3, it says: "Open fire on siptar terrorist forces only if you have reliable information that diplomatic representatives and observer missions are not present in their combat formation. Abstain from opening fire as much as possible, and only do so in case of extreme need." What does that tell us, please, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the interpreter who is interpreting into Serbian is reading the Serbian text, the original, which is right, but the English translation says -- "[In English] ... observer missions are not present in their combat formation," [Interpretation] and so on. The translation has completely omitted a particular section, and that's why I insist that you give me a recording because the translations are catastrophic and malicious. The buildings where there are no -- where there's no civilian population, that was totally omitted. And there is particular emphasis on that. Mr. Nice quoted that from the English translation. It's not in the transcript, and it says here right in front of me, and the interpreter was reading out this paragraph, too, that is to say this can be carried out "... only if the brigade commander deems this appropriate in order to neutralise targets that are a threat to human lives, such as: bunkers, buildings in which there are no civilians," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What paragraph is that? That's paragraph 3? 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 2. But, Your Honour, before we deal with that, I would --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 2 that you quoted and that I heard in Serbian from the interpreter, but in the English text that is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Milosevic, irrespective of how this is to be dealt with, I cannot allow you to say, as you said, that the interpretation is malicious. A mistake may be made, and if a mistake is made it is only human to err, and we'll do our best to correct it. But to say that it is malicious, that it was prompted by improper motives, is without foundation. Now, what are you saying? You're saying that the interpreter omitted a reference to "civilians"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow what is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is missing? Let us just have it clear. What is missing? What is missing from the interpretation, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you that I heard the interpreter reading the Serbian translation from the document. What is in the Serbian text is not in the transcript. I did not listen to Serbian and English at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what exactly is missing? What's the phrase that's missing that you're complaining of?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is missing in the transcript are the words that refer to the fact that only facilities where there are no civilians can be targeted. This civilian population reference was completely omitted. This is the commander's order, saying that people were moving about unannounced and that therefore fire cannot be opened, that only firing targets can be engaged, but to be sure not to open fire at facilities where there is civilian population. And that is a very important thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Nice, you were reading from paragraph 2, and the interpreter was interpreting what you were reading from paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That may be the -- that may be the problem. The passage that you said was omitted is in our text in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not omitted. I don't think it's omitted. I checked the transcript and it appeared, so I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it seems to me that after this diversion it's clear that the text is in both documents. As far as I'm concerned, I read it out, and with your leave I'll press on with the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to back, then, to what I was actually asking you about, Mr. Delic, which is paragraph 3. And in case you've forgotten it, I'll read it slowly and in full. "Open fire on Siptar terrorist forces only if you have reliable information that diplomatic representatives and observer missions are not present in their combat formation. Abstain from opening fire as much as possible and only do so in case of extreme need." Why was it necessary to change what you would be saying was entirely lawful conduct because of the presence of international observers apart, of course, from to respect their safety?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are just taking one order here, whereas there are dozens of orders governing the opening of fire on Siptar terrorists. This is quite normal if diplomatic representatives are coming, and our state is answerable for their security, we have to take care, even at the cost of Siptar terrorists targeting our units, as long as there are no losses incurred on the mission. Second, it is prohibited to fire from any of these enumerated weapons without an order directly from the corps commander. So even I as brigade commander can issue such an order. The next aim is to protect civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... focus of my question. And in case you can't remember it, I'll read it to you again. Why was it necessary to change what you would be saying was entirely lawful conduct because of the presence of international observers, apart, of course, from to respect their safety? Now, that's the question.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an undertone to your question that is unfair. You seem to imply that we acted until that time without any restriction and now we are introducing restrictions. The opening of fire was always restricted to sources of fire, to terrorists acting against our units. It was never allowed to open fire at buildings, and it says here that it is even prohibited to target a building from which terrorists are firing if there are civilians inside. And it also says that units should be contained to the maximum in opening fire. I believe this order is quite normal in any professional army, including your own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not an undertone. It was going to be the subject of my next question, and you anticipated it in your answer to a degree. This document gives the game away, doesn't it, because by July of 1998, death of Kosovo Albanians had become something that was easy to bring about from time to time and something that the police and the army were prepared to accept as an incident of what they were doing, but with observers around, you had to be more careful. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying is absolutely untrue. It has nothing to do with reality. I was there and you were not, Mr. Nice, and what you are saying are pure insinuations. The army acted in a professional manner, just as the Ministry of the Interior, at all times. And while you are speaking about the Albanians who were killed, please give me a number. How many Albanians were killed in one month, the next month, the month after next, and where? You cannot find such data because that did not happen, so the data does not exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just look at another small clip. I may have to expand this clip later, but I'll look at it now in its present form from the same film, again General Pavkovic. Sorry. It's clip number 13. I'm grateful to Ms. Dicklich.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we may need to expand on the meaning of activities, but you saw there General Pavkovic making it clear that one of the obstacles that was being faced was the presence of the eyes of the international community on what you were all doing. Did that affect the way you conducted yourself, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my conduct is concerned, whether there were any observers around or not, my conduct was always soldierly and professional, and the observers did not influence that in any way. They were an additional burden in the sense that I also had to worry about their security. And my professionalism cannot be affected by any presence of the observers and it cannot be questioned, today or in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can we then go to the next volume, please, of exhibits, tab 71. This is still in July of 1998, and it's an order, I think, from your brigade, and it relates to the -- I'm so sorry. You haven't found it. This document, if you have it there, I see it's highlighted so -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. oh, no. Tab 71. I see you've highlighted it, so you've read it. Indeed, it looks like you've highlighted the same part I'm interested in. It says: "Since numerous delegations of diplomatic representatives, monitoring missions, representatives of humanitarian organisations, local and foreign journalists are expected to visit certain areas in Kosovo according to their own plans and without advance notice, in order to prevent opening fire on sectors where these people might find themselves ... I hereby order: "1. I hereby strictly forbid opening fire with 122-millimetre calibre artillery pieces and 100-millimetre tank guns without the authorisation of this command." May we take it, then, that you had been spending those rounds in the period and up until the 9th of July, 1998? Large calibre weapons --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, this order of mine is associated with the order you read previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My order is a follow-up of the order dated the 7th of July. I received an order from the corps command, and I'm writing an order to my units. I do not mention calibres others -- other than those I have. And this is the month of July. Up to the 17th of July, no tank projectile and no artillery shell was fired from my brigade. So until the 18th, actually, of July. And you see that the order is very similar to or identical to the order I received from the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have we -- we've passed, I think, the date of your meeting with General Perisic that you wanted to tell us about, but perhaps we'll just make available to you first of all his letter of the 23rd of July of 1998, and you can comment on that. And then if there's something relevant in your meeting in May, then of course you must have an opportunity to tell us about that too. This is already an exhibit, twice, I think. 469, tab 23 is one instance. It's a long letter. You're familiar with it, I assume?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... some detail --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I was not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Having analysed," he says, your relations with the Yugoslav army, "I find it necessary to present you with a few facts ..." Next paragraph: "I hope you've been convinced of its high military and political awareness," et cetera. I move to the next paragraph to save time: "However, we would not be correct and sincere in the fateful circumstances if as professionals who have preserved the army and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under conditions of which you are aware, we were not to furnish you with the following negative facts: "Constant tendency to use the VJ outside the institutions of the system; "Separating VJ units from the Yugoslav army; "Attempting to command VJ units by unauthorised persons; "Bypassing levels of command in official talks with VJ members; "Conducting personal policies on an illegitimate basis and groundless foundations; "Supplying material extra-legally ..." Before we look on, does that fit with your understanding of events in the summer of 1998, that there was using the VJ outside the system, separating units from the army, bypassing levels of command?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The knowledge that I gained on the ground is quite contrary to what is written here, but I could only speak about the level of the Pristina Corps and the level of my brigade. None of these things that are written here apply. Perhaps this is a reference to some higher levels. Everything that was done on the level of the Pristina Corps and my brigade was in keeping with the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says this under the next paragraph, specific examples: "The tendency to use the VJ outside the institutions of the system. "The situation in Kosovo could have been avoided by the introduction of a state of" - must be state of emergency - "promptly on the 20th of April, 1998 - when I submitted a written proposal to you ... Since this was not accepted by you, the situation has escalated and so representatives of the Ministry of the Interior, you too, sought the use of the VJ, some smaller units were used directly and indirectly, which is from a legal aspect against the law..." Now, Mr. Delic, two points: First of all, does that accord with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know my unit, and this does not reflect the reality. I believe that Mr. Perisic overstepped his authority as Chief of General Staff because he seems to be lecturing here about state affairs. He is a soldier, not a politician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to introduce a state of emergency --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... come back in a minute. Pausing there. Do you remember I asked you yesterday whether you, if you'd been instructed by Pavkovic in the year 2000 without a state of emergency to take the tanks onto the street, you said you wouldn't, you would have disobeyed the order. Are you saying it was wrong for General Perisic to draw to this accused's attention the legal requirements for the situation in which he found himself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His powers including report -- included reporting to Mr. Milosevic about the situation on the ground and to submit proposals but not to lecture. This letter sounds as if a subordinate were lecturing his superior, and at the end of the day, Mr. Perisic was a traitor to his country. He betrayed his country, and I don't want to discuss him any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you? Well, you'll answer the questions, if you'd be so good, that I'll put to you on the basis of this letter. "(b): So that the relevant and professional conclusions of the session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 9th of June, 1998 might be implemented, we requested the FRY government to assure us (by proclaiming one of the states: Of emergency, or immediate threat of war or war) legitimate material and financial resources ... that has not, to date, been done, which means that any engagement of the VJ in combat operations outside the border zone ... is still illegal - with possible consequences unforeseeable." In that paragraph was your Chief of General Staff not seeking to support the army, ensure that it was properly resourced and activated according to the law?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was always engaged in accordance with the law. The rules of service envisage engagement of the army in several situations. First, in the case of natural or major disasters on the territory, in which case the decision on the use of the army can be taken by the brigade commander. Second, in case of the holding of large rallies, sports events, and similar. And third, the army of Yugoslavia may be used in fighting terrorist and renegade groups, and the army did that. So that is envisaged by the rules of service, and that does not require the introduction of any state of emergency. The state of emergency is something to be proclaimed by the Assembly. One man cannot lecture the Assembly. He can only suggest, and that is linked with a number of others, international, political and other problems that are associated with a state of emergency, which in itself restricts the rights of citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The rules of service, as you will be able to confirm, are internal military secret documents and they're not public documents, are they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? Which rules of engagement? There are no such rules. There are combat rules, and there is a rule of service. There is a rule of service, and you certainly have it here. I even think that my administration submitted it to you through the National Council for Cooperation, the rules of service for the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've suggested that the army could be engaged in these circumstances legitimately under the rules of service. That's what our translation says. I'm going to suggest to you that the rules of service were a secret document, and even if they were signed by this accused they couldn't pass or surpass the constitution. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule of service is not a secret document. It is an internal document. That means it has the lowest level of confidentiality of all the documents we have. That means it may be available to institutions other than the army. It is not at all secret. There is nothing secret about it because every soldier who comes to do his military service can read it so that he can behave in the way required by the rule of service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go down in General Perisic's letter, because the Court has seen it before. We don't need to go through it all, but of course if you want to look at it, you're entitled to do so I think in these circumstances, but let's go down to paragraph 3, shall we, where he turns to the particular problem of attempting to command the VJ by unauthorised persons. He says this: "The constant desire of members of the MUP that we subordinate a VJ unit to them causes disputes if it is not permitted them, if one is granted them then it is used purposelessly and unprofessionally, which proves counterproductive. The best example is Decani and Orahovac."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can stop here for a moment, because Orahovac is in my area. What happened in Decani, I don't know, but as far as Orahovac is concerned, I know all about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, please tell us, because however much you may disapprove of the Chief of General Staff lecturing this accused, it's hard to think of him, is it not, writing something without a foundation in fact. So what was he in July 1998 writing about so far as Orahovac was concerned? You must be able to help us.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this point A, one is supposed to conclude that the liberation of Orahovac town involved the MUP commanding my unit. Mr. Nice, not you, not Perisic, nobody in this courtroom was in Orahovac. Only I was, both on the 18th and the 19th, and I know what happened minute by minute. Perisic did not clarify the issue of Orahovac in detail. He just mentioned it in passing. My unit was there, and directly under my command supported MUP forces which liberated Orahovac from terrorists. I even have a video recording here about the liberation of Orahovac. One part was recorded by the Siptars, and another part was recorded from our side. There were certain forces of the MUP there. There was a part of my unit acting in support. At no point did anybody from the MUP, because I was there as brigade commander and the MUP was represented only by lower-ranking commanding officers, their chief of secretariat was in Prizren, I was commanding my unit. All that MUP could do was to ask me to neutralise the source of fire that was in their way. To liberate a town with a population of 50.000, only 12 projectiles were fired from a T-55 tank, only 12, whereas Siptar forces, and we probably have this figure here, had 1.500 men. 150 Serbs had been kidnapped between the 17th and the 19th. How can Mr. Perisic write something about it when he wasn't there? With all due respect, after all, he was my chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the circumstances I was allowing the witness to run along, but I think I'm going to bring it to a conclusion with this question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken now of events between the 17th and 19th. That's the 17th and 19th of which month?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And help us, please. Have you set out these documents that relate to this event in the papers that we've got?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map, the order, the analysis, all the documents about this event exist, but not here perhaps, I have to check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We now see, you see, from your long answer, which I did not interrupt, that in the apparent liberation of this place your group, in collaboration, cooperation, or subordination to the MUP, fired 12 projectiles from a tank. Did you not think that might be material we'd like to see in this Court, investigating as we are the role of the army?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to know, this was an operation conducted professionally. To liberate a town with 40 or 50.000 population with 12 projectiles, I would really like to see a NATO force that could do it the same way. So if we don't have this document here, and if the Trial Chamber should insist, considering that I have received a waiver from the Official Secrets Act, if you want my documentation from Belgrade, I will try to get it. The complete documentation for the 18th --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... enough on this point. I don't want to be offensive to anybody, but I think the point has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to General Perisic's letter and what's said there about Decani and Orahovac, can I remind you of something, or tell you of something that was given in the evidence of Mr. Crosland, who had discussions with General Dimitrijevic at the time, and he said that it was obvious, clear to him, that Perisic and Dimitrijevic were not fully informed as to what was going on on the ground in Kosovo, being excluded from the operational chain of command which went directly from General Pavkovic to this accused, Milosevic, and to Sainovic. Now, what do you say to that? He was your commander, Pavkovic. Did he have a direct line of command that bypassed Perisic and Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dimitrijevic is absolutely not in the chain of command. General Pavkovic has nothing with Dimitrijevic. As for Perisic, General Pavkovic does not have direct communication with Perisic either, because General Pavkovic has communication with the commander of the 3rd Army. Let me just tell you that at this time and all the way up to the month of October there was the forward command post of the army in Pristina, and it was headed by Lieutenant Colonel General Simic. Mr. Pavkovic could not make a single decision without that decision having been approved by General Simic who is the Chief of Staff the 3rd Army and the deputy commander of the 3rd Army of General Samardzic. So the chain of command was absolutely not harmed in any way. The security service is not in the chain of command. General Dimitrijevic, therefore, is not there. There is the vertical chain up to brigade level that links up all the security organs. And quite simply it was not envisaged that commanders of any unit, corps, et cetera, would have any kind of obligation to report to Dimitrijevic as head of that service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... simple. As far as you were concerned, was it the case that you could see that Pavkovic had a direct line of command that bypassed Perisic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Insofar as paragraph 3 A of the letter is concerned, of course Perisic should have had access to any intelligence he wanted, shouldn't he? The line of reporting would lead to him ultimately and he could have access to it if he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... complaining about something that's happened immediately in your area of command contemporaneously there and then on 23rd of July, according to your account, four days after things happened. How could General Perisic have got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic is here, so ask him. I think that I have relevant documentation for this case. If it is important, we can deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember -- ah, you mean you've got some other documentation not here in Court that relates to this topic? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I already took the largest number of documents that I thought could assist me in cross-examination so that I would not be talking just like that but that I could document every word I say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, then, you've come armed with additional documentation to meet the questions you have forecast I'm going to ask but they haven't been included in the original 629 documents presented to us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, "armed" might be an unfortunate word, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Equipped.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my own documentation. The legal advisors selected documentation in accordance with their own way of thinking on particular topics that they asked me to prepare on. Had I been in a position to select documentation, I would have taken a lot more documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we going to be able to know in general or by an index or something or other what it is you've got that is all this additional material or are we just going to wait for it to be produced right at the end of the exercise? Can you tell us what you've got?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documentation that I have is documentation that pertains to my unit. Every document that we use in this courtroom will be submitted to the representatives of the Defence if that is deemed necessary for this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's going to create an interesting problem, but we'll come to it a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember you were asked a lot of questions about the Joint Command, both by the Court and by me yesterday and last week. Will you now look at paragraph 3(B). "The attempt by the civilian part of the staff to command the corps. The corps commander is responsible for assessing the situation and for planning VJ and MUP operations in cooperation with the civilian part of the staff and the MUP, for forwarding it to Sainovic and Minic for them to distribute assignments to all except the Pristina Corps. In practice, the commander of the Pristina Corps plans what he has been ordered to do, and this is at the request of Sainovic and Minic and the MUP, and so turns into something like a service of theirs --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The page on the ELMO needs to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. I failed to observe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... so it turns into something like a service of theirs for planning and execution. Since it is his wish and that of all of us that the plan be realised if others will not or cannot, he executes it with the Pristina Corps units, which leads to an illegitimate, unsystematic and inadequate utilisation of VJ units, thereby wrecking the system; they split up the units, expend them, tie them down, and so if it is actually necessary to use the corps according to the regulations on its use in combat, it may not be possible to use it. There are we see Sainovic and Minic, the civilians, and a reference to the Pristina Corps and the way it was circumventing the rules. What was General Perisic referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through this point we can only see the vanity of Mr. Perisic. There could not have been any illegal use of the corps at any point in time. General Simic was in Pristina. That is the next officer in the chain of command above the Pristina Corps. General Pavkovic, when he'd go to these meetings, would have to tell General Simic why he was asked to go to a meeting. If he took upon himself an obligation, or if he was supposed to engage any unit of the Pristina Corps, then General Simic had to approve that. General Simic is the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army of General Samardzic, who is the first person in the chain of command right after General Perisic. So General Simic either allowed the use of some unit or did not allow the use of some unit. General Pavkovic could not use a single unit of the corps without General Simic if it was supposed to act in concert with the MUP. My unit was never used illegally. It was never given to anyone else to command. The first use of my unit was on the 18th of July during the liberation of Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me make a simple suggestion to you and then we're going to move on from this letter. You had, I must suggest to you, the greatest difficulty in explaining to the learned Judges when they asked you questions, or to me, what the chain of command was where the word "Joint Command" was used, and the reason you had that difficulty is because you knew you were responding to an illicit and improper body that had no rights to command you. Is that the truth? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the other way around. I have no difficulty whatsoever in connection with the Joint Command. Please, let us take a tab out where there is reference to the Joint Command and let me show it to you again. The Joint Command the way you see it did not exist. For me, the Joint Command was the Pristina Corps from which I received my orders. Can we take tab 4 and look at an order of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd prefer us not to. You can deal with it in re-examination. I've put my point to you and I want to move on, or to be precise, I want to move back to Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I first tell you about my encounter with General Perisic, because you mentioned him, and you said that I had the opportunity of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It relates to the topic --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It directly relates to this topic. Towards the end of May, 1998, I was visited on the same day by General Perisic together with the commander of the 3rd Army. I met them in Prizren at my sports field, which was a heliodrom, a heliport at the same time. Of course, as soon as they got out of the helicopter I reported to General Perisic, saluted him, shook hands with him, and the first thing he asked me was, "How are things going, Delic?" and I said, "It's very hard. The situation in my zone is very difficult." As I was -- as we were going towards the car because we were supposed to go to my office, I said, "General, please do something. All the roads in my zone, the Djakovica-Klina-Pristina road is broken off and is held by terrorists. The Prizren-Orahovac-Malisevo road is also intercepted by the terrorists. I have information that the Suva Reka-Stimlje road will also be cut off one of these days, and apart from this communication here via Sredska, which is a bad road, I'm not going to have any links with my rear. General Samardzic used a vulgar word that I'm not going to utter now, and General Perisic said, "What do you care? Let them introduce a state of emergency and we're going to resolve it in ten days' time." I'm surprised that such a high-ranking officer of such high rank would have such an attitude of underestimation towards this kind of problem because this kind of problem could not be resolved in ten days. It couldn't even be resolved in ten months. Now, he's the one who knows how he thought it could be resolved in ten days. He didn't give me any help. This road was cut off, and I had no communication whatsoever except for that very bad road via Sredska between Metohija and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now go back to Lord Ashdown, and having seen the observations about avoiding the sight or the eyes of international observers, I make this simple suggestion to you: The problem with Lord Ashdown and his evidence is that as he was observing you from Albania through field glasses, you had no reason to know he was there, and you got caught. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing you said, the first statement of yours in relation to international observers is ludicrous. We were in our own country. We were attacked by terrorism, like London was the other day. Isn't terrorism a danger for all countries in the world? We had nothing to hide. We wanted to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your answers, otherwise we won't make much progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the way, this was dealt with at tab 37, for the Court, if it has a desire to turn to the tab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to know what you're saying about Lord Ashdown's evidence and how it is you're saying it. First of all, did you listen to his evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you said that we were caught by Lord Ashdown. According to the way you presented things here where he was in Albania, and I drew that schematic for you, he could absolutely see only one Albanian village and one that is scattered around --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to give you an opportunity to deal with this in a straightforward way, and perhaps you'd be good enough to listen to the questions. Did you listen to Lord Ashdown's evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except for this transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah. Did you read the transcript?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part that was read out to me by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that all that you've relied on in order to express the views on Lord Ashdown that you have so far expressed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was read out to me and what was said in relation to some point on the border with Albania. As for what I was asked to do, that was more than sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean as to what you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me. If I said that there was this post on the border with Albania near the village of Gegaj or near the Albanian border post Kamenica, as Lord Ashdown said, from that point you can see all of Kosovo all the way to Pristina. That is absolutely untrue. Whoever knows topography, at least, who has a bare knowledge of topography can know that not more than three or four kilometres can be seen from that point, and that is one single Albanian village, the village of Moric [as interpreted] that can be seen from there. Let me just have a look now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What map is it that you're going to be most assisted by?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the -- could the Albanian -- could the name of the Albanian village be corrected in the transcript. It's the village of Morina, the village of Moric cannot be seen. I was there -- well, not to say a hundred times but tens of times. I know every meadow in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't, please, fall into a trap or what you think is a trap, but we want to assess how you've given your evidence and what you're saying, what it amounts to. Are you saying that Lord Ashdown is definitely wrong and must be, frankly, making it up, or are you saying that he may be mistaken? And having expressed which of the views you're holding to, then tell us why.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me where Lord Ashdown was in Albania. I have an excellent knowledge of that terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Delic, I didn't. Just to get the sequence right, and that's why I want you not to be lulled into any trap, the accused gave a summary of the evidence, we suggested that it was marked on a map, and you were provided, first of all, with a map which you rejected because it was too detailed and not perhaps topographical enough. Then you were provided with a blank version of this map, and it came --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You marked on it the position where you, for whatever reason -- and perhaps you'd like to have it, just have another look at it. You marked on it yourself the position where you say Lord Ashdown was, and you then shaded in the map with areas that you said could and couldn't be seen. And just to complete the history, you explained the position to Ms. Dicklich. I asked the Court if they wanted to deal with the map then and there and they said no, in cross-examination, and I think that Ms. Dicklich took an opportunity, so that the accused couldn't be disadvantaged, to explain to him what you'd said to her. So this map was not marked by us, it was marked by you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The evidence that Lord Ashdown gave, as you understand it, was what, that he was at the village of Gegaj with a view of Junik. Is that what you understand his evidence to be?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Junik was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, you're expressing views about the accuracy of a person who has been a witness in this case, somebody who I'm sure would seek no special credit for his position and, therefore, who must be assessed objectively. I want you please to tell me, what did you understand his evidence to be? Very simple question. That he was standing where and that he saw what?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you mentioned Junik, the Trial Chamber asked me about Junik when the map was shown that the legal advisors obtained, and that map was shown on the ELMO. I was asked where Junik was, and I said that Junik was to the north, and that from the point where Lord Ashdown was it could not be seen. In the transcript in relation to Lord Ashdown, it was said that he was in Albania at the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, near the village of Gegaj, that in front he had all of Kosovo and Metohija, practically all the way to Pristina, that he saw mortar positions, and he assessed that they were 82-millimetre mortars. He saw tanks and so on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the accused suggested to you that he had a very good view of the entire area to the south of Junik. This is, in fact, what Lord Ashdown said, and I'll read it slowly, and I hope you can follow it. He said: "I journeyed from Bajram Curiju through Trepoje, along the lines here - there is a very rough track up to the border crossing here - and then followed this border crossing up to a point on the Albanian-Kosovo border ..." he marked it on the map - "... above a village which I was informed was called Gegaj ... this gave me a very good view of the whole of the south of the -- of the whole area around south of Junik. There are some small villages down here. And indeed, I could see deep into Kosovo, because this is an area of plains here, almost as far as Pristina." With that evidence in mind, we sent to Lord Ashdown a transcript of your evidence and of that map. If Mr. Prendergast would be good enough, if we could distribute first this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this exercise, I wonder if the Prosecution could produce where Lord Ashdown marked on the map so that we can see that. Apparently it was originally made an exhibit. I can't remember the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
